Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Environmental Scientist
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs, Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented, Avoid Eye Contact: Making eye contact with other people, Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Vignette:
Margaret Chen was sixty-three when it happened. She had spent thirty years as an environmental scientist, moving between field research stations and university offices, comfortable in her solitude and her work. The assault occurred at a conference in San Francisco, in a hotel corridor late at night after a reception. A colleague she had known professionally for years—someone she had trusted enough to walk back to the elevators with—had cornered her outside her room. She had tried to reason with him, then to push past him. He was stronger. It lasted perhaps ten minutes, though time had fractured in her memory into something both endless and impossibly compressed. She had frozen halfway through, her mind splitting into an observer watching her own body from somewhere near the ceiling. When he finally left, she had locked herself in the bathroom and remained there until dawn.

Fourteen years had passed since then. Margaret was now seventy-seven, and the world had become a landscape of careful calculations and hidden exits. The immediate shock had given way not to healing but to an insidious rewiring of her mind. She had begun replaying the evening obsessively, searching for the moment she could have prevented it. If she had not worn the burgundy dress. If she had not accepted the invitation to the reception. If she had not mentioned her room number during conversation. She had come to believe, with the certainty of someone who has examined every frame of a film countless times, that her own choices had opened the door to what happened. The shame of this—the conviction that her body had been violated because of something she had done—had calcified into a permanent weight she carried. What frightened her most was the thought that she remained fundamentally unsafe, that the kind of man who could do this was everywhere, waiting for her to make another mistake.

Within months of the assault, she had developed rituals. Before entering any space—a grocery store, her university office, a restaurant—she would pause and locate the exits. She needed to know where the doors were, which windows might open, whether there was a back route. At home, she had installed new locks and kept her bedroom door barricaded. At night, she lay awake listening to the sounds of her house, alert to any noise that might signal an intruder. Her sleep had become fragmented, haunted by the sensation of footsteps approaching, by the phantom feeling of hands on her body. She would wake gasping, her heart hammering, uncertain whether minutes or hours had passed. Physical contact had become intolerable. Her sister, visiting from Portland, had tried to embrace her at the airport, and Margaret had stiffened, her body flooding with panic. She had stepped back, offered an awkward pat on the arm instead. The hurt in her sister's eyes had stayed with her, but the thought of being held—of anyone's hands on her—made her skin crawl with a shame so profound she could barely articulate it. Even the thought of intimacy, of being vulnerable with another person in that way, felt like stepping toward a cliff edge.

Her career had contracted around these constraints. She had retired early from fieldwork, citing age, though the truth was more complicated. Open landscapes—the marshes and grasslands she had once loved—now felt exposing, indefensible. She had shifted to lab-based analysis, work she could do alone in controlled spaces where she could lock the door and position herself with clear sightlines. Her colleagues had noticed the change, the way she now declined social gatherings, the way she would not make eye contact during department meetings or stand with her back to the room. Some had attributed it to age or temperament. None knew. The hypervigilance that had once served a purpose—scanning for threat, cataloging escape routes—had become the texture of her daily existence. Every sound in the hallway outside her lab made her shoulders tense. Every unexpected knock at her door sent adrenaline coursing through her body. She was certain that danger was present, waiting, that her age and her solitude made her an easy target.

What had finally brought her to seek help was a moment of unexpected clarity. Her granddaughter, visiting for her birthday, had asked why Grandmother didn't like hugs. Margaret had no answer that wouldn't burden the child with adult darkness. But the question had cracked something open—the recognition that she was not just surviving the aftermath of the assault, but actively preventing herself from living. She was afraid of men, afraid of touch, afraid of being seen. She believed, with a certainty born from years of rumination, that the harm that had found her once would find her again. And she believed, most painfully, that it had been her fault to begin with. At her first therapy session, Margaret sat in a chair positioned where she could see the door. She was afraid, still, of what help might mean. But she was also, for the first time in fourteen years, willing to try.
